title: Stock market foundations
description: Get familiar with shares, ownership, and how stock prices move.
takeaways: Understand what a share of stock represents.
Recognize that prices can rise or fall.
Know that dividends and investment returns are not guaranteed.

scenes.title: What is a share?
scenes.text: A share of stock represents an ownership interest in a company. A shareholder owns a small piece of that business.

scenes.title: Why companies issue shares
scenes.text: Companies may sell shares to raise money for their work and growth. Ownership does not promise a profit.

scenes.title: Why the price moves
scenes.text: A stock price changes as buyers and sellers respond to company news, expectations, and broader market conditions.

scenes.title: A simple gain or loss
scenes.text: If a share is bought for $50 and sold for $58, the difference is $8 before costs. Selling for $42 instead means an $8 loss.

scenes.title: Dividends are possible
scenes.text: Some companies pay part of their earnings to shareholders as dividends. Payments can change or stop, and many stocks pay none.

scenes.title: Know the risk
scenes.text: A share can lose value. If a company struggles, an investor can lose part or all of the money invested in its stock.

scenes.title: Spread your exposure
scenes.text: Diversification spreads money across investments. It can reduce some risk but cannot guarantee against losses.

scenes.title: Put it together
scenes.text: Remember the core ideas: a share is ownership, its market price changes, dividends are uncertain, and risk is always present.

extraLessons.title: Returns, dividends, and real costs
extraLessons.description: Work through a stock return and see how costs and dividends change the result.
takeaways: Separate a price change from total return.
Subtract trading costs in a simple example.
Remember that dividends and returns are uncertain.

scenes.title: Price return
scenes.text: The price difference is the sale price minus the purchase price. A higher sale price alone does not tell the full story.

scenes.title: An example purchase
scenes.text: Imagine buying 10 shares for $20 each. The purchase costs $200 before any trading fees.

scenes.title: An example sale
scenes.text: If the shares are sold for $23 each, the sale proceeds are $230. The price gain before costs is $30.

scenes.title: Include costs
scenes.text: Suppose total purchase and sale costs are $4. The example gain after those costs is $26, before taxes.

scenes.title: Consider a dividend
scenes.text: A company may pay a dividend during ownership. A $0.50 dividend per share on 10 shares would add $5 before taxes.

scenes.title: A loss scenario
scenes.text: If the sale price is $17 per share, proceeds are $170. The price loss is $30 before costs or dividends.

scenes.title: No guaranteed payout
scenes.text: A company can reduce or stop dividends. Stock prices also move in either direction; a previous gain predicts nothing.

scenes.title: Check the full picture
scenes.text: Record purchase price, sale price, number of shares, costs, and any distributions before describing a return.

extraLessons.title: Research a company before investing
extraLessons.description: Practice a beginner checklist for understanding a business and its risks.
takeaways: Explain how the business earns money.
Check reliable company information and risks.
Avoid making decisions from one headline.

scenes.title: Begin with the business
scenes.text: Ask what the company sells, who its customers are, and where its revenue comes from before looking at the share price.

scenes.title: Look at financial reports
scenes.text: Public companies publish reports with financial results and risk discussions. Read them instead of relying on a headline.

scenes.title: Revenue and profit
scenes.text: Revenue is money earned from sales. Profit remains after expenses. Growing sales do not guarantee growing profit.

scenes.title: Debt matters
scenes.text: Borrowing may help a company operate or expand, but debt also creates obligations. Look at the business in context.

scenes.title: Read the risk section
scenes.text: Competition, costs, regulation, and other events can change a company’s outlook. Risks differ by business.

scenes.title: Compare over time
scenes.text: One quarter may be unusual. Comparing several periods can reveal changes, though past performance cannot predict the future.

scenes.title: Question the source
scenes.text: A confident stock tip is not evidence. Check the source and whether the person may benefit from your decision.

scenes.title: Write a short summary
scenes.text: In your own words, explain what the company does, one strength, one risk, and what information you still need.

title: Reading price charts
description: Learn what the body, wicks, and timeframe of a candle tell you.
takeaways: Identify the open, high, low, and close of a candle.
Read a candle’s body and wicks.
Check which time period each candle represents.

scenes.title: Four prices in one candle
scenes.text: A candlestick summarizes the open, high, low, and close for one selected time period.

scenes.title: Start with the body
scenes.text: The candle body spans the opening and closing prices. Its length shows the difference between those two prices.

scenes.title: Then read the wicks
scenes.text: The upper wick reaches the period high. The lower wick reaches the period low, beyond the body.

scenes.title: Direction and color
scenes.text: A close above the open is often shown in green; a close below is often red. Chart color settings can vary.

scenes.title: Choose the timeframe
scenes.text: A one-minute candle covers one minute. A one-day candle covers one day. Check the scale before drawing conclusions.

scenes.title: Try a worked example
scenes.text: Suppose open is $50, high is $54, low is $49, and close is $52. The body runs from $50 to $52; wicks reach $49 and $54.

scenes.title: What a candle cannot tell you
scenes.text: A candle shows a past price range, not what will happen next. One candle alone is a limited picture.

scenes.title: Read it back
scenes.text: Identify the timeframe, then find open and close in the body and high and low at the tips of the wicks.

extraLessons.title: Timeframes and price context
extraLessons.description: Compare the same price movement across different chart timeframes.
takeaways: Read the timeframe and price axis first.
Understand how candles group prices.
Avoid predictions from a single candle.

scenes.title: Check the chart label
scenes.text: Before interpreting a chart, identify the instrument, the dates shown, and the time interval represented by each mark.

scenes.title: One period, four prices
scenes.text: A daily candle summarizes one trading day. An hourly candle summarizes one hour of prices.

scenes.title: Zoom changes the picture
scenes.text: A short chart may show a sharp move. A longer view can reveal that the move is small relative to earlier changes.

scenes.title: Axes set the scale
scenes.text: Read the price values on the vertical axis. A narrow displayed range can make a modest move look dramatic.

scenes.title: Compare equal intervals
scenes.text: A series of candles is only comparable after checking that the interval stays the same throughout the view.

scenes.title: Gaps can appear
scenes.text: A new period can open above or below the previous close. The chart may show a gap between those prices.

scenes.title: Past does not predict
scenes.text: A chart is a record of earlier transactions. A visual pattern alone cannot promise the next price.

scenes.title: Read the context
scenes.text: State the timeframe, start and end dates, and observed price range before offering an interpretation.

extraLessons.title: Volume and chart limitations
extraLessons.description: Learn what trading volume counts and what it cannot explain about a price move.
takeaways: Define volume as traded shares for a period.
Compare volume across matching periods.
Separate observation from a trading prediction.

scenes.title: What volume measures
scenes.text: Stock trading volume is the number of shares traded over a chosen period. It does not count unique investors.

scenes.title: Match the periods
scenes.text: An hourly volume bar counts activity for that hour. Compare bars using the same length of time.

scenes.title: Price and activity
scenes.text: A price move with high volume shows many shares traded. The bar alone does not explain why traders acted.

scenes.title: A low-volume example
scenes.text: A price can move while few shares trade. Do not assume that a quiet bar means the price will reverse.

scenes.title: Read the labels
scenes.text: Check whether the chart reports shares, contracts, or another measure. Check whether the period is complete.

scenes.title: News can shift interest
scenes.text: Company announcements and broad market events may change both price and volume. Verify the actual event.

scenes.title: Limits of a chart
scenes.text: Historical price and volume do not reveal every investor’s reason or guarantee a future direction.

scenes.title: Use a careful summary
scenes.text: Describe what changed, the timeframe, and the volume shown. Then separately note what remains unknown.

title: Order types & risk
description: Understand three common order types and their trade-offs.
takeaways: Distinguish market, limit, and stop orders.
Understand why an execution price can change.
Recognize that a limit order may never be filled.

scenes.title: An order is an instruction
scenes.text: An order tells a broker to try to buy or sell. The type you select changes the trade-off between speed and price control.

scenes.title: Market order
scenes.text: A market order seeks prompt execution at available prices. It does not guarantee the price you will receive.

scenes.title: Buy limit order
scenes.text: A buy limit of $50 sets $50 as the most you will pay per share. The order may not execute if a seller is not available at that price.

scenes.title: Sell limit order
scenes.text: A sell limit of $55 sets $55 as the least you will accept per share. The order can remain unfilled.

scenes.title: Stop order
scenes.text: When the stop price is reached, a stop order becomes a market order. The eventual execution price can differ from the stop price.

scenes.title: Stop-limit order
scenes.text: A stop-limit order becomes a limit order once triggered. It adds price control but may never execute.

scenes.title: Review before submitting
scenes.text: Check the action, number of shares, order type, and price fields. Broker choices and order duration may vary.

scenes.title: Compare the trade-offs
scenes.text: Market focuses on execution, limit focuses on a price boundary, and stop adds a trigger. No order type eliminates market risk.

extraLessons.title: Bid, ask, and the spread
extraLessons.description: Read a quoted market and see why the displayed price may differ from a fill.
takeaways: Identify the bid and ask.
Calculate a simple spread.
Recognize that quotes can change before execution.

scenes.title: Two sides of a quote
scenes.text: The bid is a displayed buying price. The ask is a displayed selling price. The values can change quickly.

scenes.title: A simple quote
scenes.text: Suppose a stock displays a $49.90 bid and a $50.10 ask. The quoted difference, or spread, is $0.20.

scenes.title: Buying at the ask
scenes.text: A market buy generally seeks available shares from sellers. The current ask is a useful reference, not a promised fill.

scenes.title: Selling at the bid
scenes.text: A market sell generally seeks an available buyer. The current bid is a reference and can change.

scenes.title: The spread is a cost
scenes.text: Buying at $50.10 and immediately selling at $49.90 would lose $0.20 per share in this simple unchanged-quote example.

scenes.title: Size and movement
scenes.text: A displayed quote may cover only some shares. A larger order or fast-moving market may reach different available prices.

scenes.title: Limit price control
scenes.text: A limit order sets a price boundary. It may sit unfilled when the market never reaches an available matching price.

scenes.title: Review before sending
scenes.text: Check the bid, ask, quantity, order type, and the possibility that the quote changes before execution.

extraLessons.title: Planning risk before an order
extraLessons.description: Use a hypothetical order to practice sizing, price boundaries, and review.
takeaways: Calculate a basic exposure amount.
Understand stop execution limits.
Review the order and risk before submitting.

scenes.title: Start with exposure
scenes.text: If you buy 5 shares at $40, the starting purchase amount is $200 before costs. Decide what loss you can afford.

scenes.title: Price can fall
scenes.text: A fall from $40 to $35 is a $5 loss per share, or $25 on 5 shares before any costs. Losses can be larger.

scenes.title: Stops have limits
scenes.text: A stop order becomes a market order when triggered. Its eventual execution price may be worse than the stop price.

scenes.title: A stop-limit trade-off
scenes.text: A stop-limit order adds a limit price after the trigger, but the order might never fill if prices move past it.

scenes.title: Diversify thoughtfully
scenes.text: Putting all funds into one stock concentrates risk. Spreading exposure may reduce some risk without removing it.

scenes.title: Check order details
scenes.text: Verify buy or sell, ticker, number of shares, order type, entered prices, and the broker’s displayed estimate.

scenes.title: Plan for uncertainty
scenes.text: Prices, fees, and available liquidity can change. A plan should allow for outcomes beyond the example numbers.

scenes.title: Pause and summarize
scenes.text: State your order, expected exposure, main risk, and why the chosen order type fits your goal before submitting.
